doc.title: Dave Frishberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Pop songwriters and the minor seventh changed jazz
summary: He argues the pop songs of Kern, Berlin and Gershwin, and the minor seventh chord, shaped jazz and bebop, criticizing Ken Burns' documentary.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Of the 20s, 30s, 40s, the golden, I mean Jerome Kern, Sigmund Romberg, Victor Herbert, Jerome Kern, Irving Berlin, Richard Rodgers, George Gershwin, that’s what changed jazz. That’s what opened the jazz musicians’ ears. That’s how jazz evolved. It was never referred to once in Ken Burns’ documentary by the way. Not once was that ever mentioned. The food of us jazz players, all of the jazz players, was the work of the greatest pop songwriters we’ve ever known and thank God we all, everybody coincided in the 1920s or 1930s. It was a lot deeper and a lot more musically oriented than Ken Burns’ thing would suggest. The Ken Burns thing was heavy on the sociology, light on the musicology. The minor seventh chord had more to do with jazz sounding the way it does than the blues does. But the minor seventh chord is not that easy to describe or make © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

dramatic. You know what I mean? Where would Charlie Parker be if it weren’t for “All the Things You Are” and Jerome Kern, who defined the chordal movement of bebop with that song. That whole song is about bebop and where bebop went. The way he manipulated harmonies and then melody, and the way he harmonized that whole thing opened up jazz musicians’ ears all over the place, including a genius or two like Charlie Parker or Lester Young. The minor seventh is what changed jazz, okay?

Exactly. Because of where it led the ear. And the minor seventh was a device of the pop song composers. It was a device of Ravel I suppose, but I’m talking about the pop songwriters like even the unschooled ones were using the minor seventh like Irving Berlin. The trained ones like Kern were using it too as part of their arsenal. It was the two chord, the minor seventh. That’s what changed jazz. That’s why jazz grew up the way it did. That’s my feeling.
